sections.h: Psalm 69: curses from the one who suffers for God
sections.b:
Psalm 69 is the curse psalm the New Testament uses most. Its speaker is mocked because "zeal for your house has eaten me up" (Psalm 69:9), and after a long lament he asks that his enemies' table become a trap, their eyes grow dark and their names be wiped out of the scroll of life (Psalm 69:22–28). The targets are those who "hunt down the one you have struck" (Psalm 69:26). Paul applies the table and the darkened eyes to Israel's partial hardening, and then at once denies that it is final (Romans 11:9–11); Peter applies the deserted camp to Judas (Acts 1:20). The psalm moves straight from curse to praise and to the rebuilding of Zion (Psalm 69:30–36).

Psalm 58 is harsher still, and aims at corrupt judges: broken teeth, a melting snail, the righteous washing their feet in blood (Psalm 58:6–10). Its goal is the confession that "a God exists who judges on the earth" (Psalm 58:11). It is one of the three psalms the Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves out. Psalm 59 adds a strange request: "Do not kill them, or my people may forget" (Psalm 59:11), which Augustine applied to the Jewish people, a reading modern churches have rejected.

sections.h: Psalms 56–72: the end of Book Two
sections.b: Book Two closes with a run of David psalms (Psalms 56–65, 68–70), five of them called miktam (Psalms 56–60), and several with story titles tying them to David's flight from Saul and his wars (Psalms 56, 57, 59, 60, 63). Psalms 66 and 67 have no author, Psalm 71 has no title at all, and the book ends with Psalm 72 "Of Solomon", a doxology and the note "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse" (Psalm 72:18–20). Two passages appear twice in the Psalter: Psalm 57:7–11 and Psalm 60:5–12 form Psalm 108, and Psalm 70 repeats Psalm 40:13–17.
sections.refs: Psalm 56:0; Psalm 60:0; Psalm 72:18–20; Psalm 108:1–13; Psalm 70:1–5; Psalm 40:13–17

sections.b: Psalm 70 is the clearest test case for the Elohistic Psalter. It repeats Psalm 40:13–17, and where Psalm 40 has "the LORD", Psalm 70 mostly has "God" (Psalm 70:1, 4, 5), though "LORD" survives twice (Psalm 70:1, 5). The same holds for Psalm 108, which combines Psalm 57:7–11 and Psalm 60:5–12 outside the Elohistic Psalter but keeps their "God" almost everywhere (but "the LORD" at Psalm 108:3). Psalm 68 shows the editing at its densest, with "God" more than twenty times and "Yah" and "LORD" kept in old formulas (Psalm 68:4, 16, 18, 20, 26).

sections.h: Psalm 72: the king who defends the poor
sections.b: Psalm 72 asks God to give the king his justice, so that he defends the poor and saves the needy (Psalm 72:1–4, 12–14). The Targum makes its first line a prayer for "King Messiah", and the Talmud reads the verb of Psalm 72:17 as the Messiah's name, Yinnon (Sanhedrin 98b). Christians read the kings with gifts (Psalm 72:10–11) with the Magi (Matthew 2:11) and the psalm as the reign of Christ. Both traditions agree on its measure: the true son of David is known by what he does for the needy.

sections.h: Prayers for the king in Psalms 61, 63 and 72
sections.b: Three psalms of Book Two pray for the king. Psalm 61 asks long life for him and a throne before God forever (Psalm 61:6–7); Psalm 63 ends "And the king will be glad in God" (Psalm 63:11); and Psalm 72 sets out the king's task: justice for the poor, rescue for the needy and the breaking of the oppressor (Psalm 72:1–4, 12–14). In these psalms the king's long reign and wide rule depend on his righteousness, which is first of all God's gift (Psalm 72:1).

Psalm 72 is one of two psalms with Solomon's name (with Psalm 127). Its title can mean "by" or "for" him. Its gold of Sheba, rule from the River, and justice for the poor recall Solomon's prayer for wisdom to judge (1 Kings 3:9) and the queen of Sheba's visit (1 Kings 10:1–10). Placed after the psalm for Solomon, the note "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse" (Psalm 72:20) marks the passing of the crown from father to son.

Psalm 72 prays that the kings of Sheba and Seba will offer gifts and that Sheba's gold will be given to the king (Psalm 72:10, 15). The lines recall the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon (1 Kings 10:1–10) and were read by Christians with the Magi's gold and frankincense (Matthew 2:11; Isaiah 60:6).

Five psalms in this stretch have titles that link them to scenes in David's life: Gath (Psalm 56:0; 1 Samuel 21:10–15), the cave (Psalm 57:0), the watch on his house (Psalm 59:0; 1 Samuel 19:11), the wars with Aram and Edom (Psalm 60:0; 2 Samuel 8), and the wilderness of Judah (Psalm 63:0). The title of Psalm 60 gives twelve thousand Edomites killed, where 2 Samuel 8:13 and 1 Chronicles 18:12 give eighteen thousand. Several titles name tunes: "A Silent Dove Far Away" (Psalm 56:0), "Do Not Destroy" (Psalms 57–59), "Lily of the Testimony" (Psalm 60:0) and "Lilies" (Psalm 69:0). Psalm 71 has no title in the Hebrew.

sections.b: Psalm 56 says God has counted the singer's wanderings and put his tears in a bottle, "Are they not in your scroll?" (Psalm 56:8). Psalm 69 asks that the enemies be wiped out of "the scroll of life" (Psalm 69:28), a register of the living, like Moses' "your book" (Exodus 32:32–33). Revelation takes up the image as the book of those who belong to the Lamb (Revelation 3:5).

The New Testament reads Psalm 69 as a pattern for Jesus' suffering: zeal for God's house (John 2:17), hatred without cause (John 15:25), insults borne for God (Romans 15:3), and vinegar for his thirst (Matthew 27:34, 48; John 19:28–29). The psalm's speaker also confesses his own foolishness (Psalm 69:5), which shows that the pattern is not a one-to-one prediction: the righteous sufferer's story is taken up and completed in Jesus.
sections.refs: Psalm 69:4–9; Psalm 69:21; John 2:17; John 15:25; Romans 15:3; John 19:28–29

sections.b: Psalms 69, 70 and 72 return again and again to the poor. The singer of Psalms 69 and 70 calls himself "poor" (Psalm 69:29) and "poor and needy" (Psalm 70:5), and says the LORD "listens to the needy" (Psalm 69:33). Psalm 72 makes the defense of the poor the reason for the king's whole reign: he will rescue the needy who cry for help, and their blood will be precious in his eyes (Psalm 72:12–14).

sections.h: Psalms 58 and 72: corrupt judges and the just king
sections.b: Two psalms of Book Two face each other. Psalm 58 accuses those who should give justice of weighing out violence with their hands (Psalm 58:2) and asks God to break their teeth; Psalm 72 prays for a king who will judge the afflicted in justice and break the oppressor (Psalm 72:2, 4). Both end in the same hope, that God's justice will be known on the earth (Psalm 58:11; Psalm 72:19).

In Psalm 68 the high peaks of Bashan look with envy at Zion, "the mountain God wanted for his home" (Psalm 68:16). God comes from Sinai to it with his chariots, so that "Sinai is in the holy place" (Psalm 68:17), and kings bring gifts to his temple above Jerusalem (Psalm 68:29). Psalm 69 ends with the promise "For God will save Zion" (Psalm 69:35).

Psalm 68 calls God "the One of Sinai" (Psalm 68:8), as the Song of Deborah does (Judges 5:5), and pictures him marching from Sinai to Zion so that Sinai's holiness comes into the sanctuary (Psalm 68:17). Jewish tradition reads Psalm 68:18 of Moses going up Sinai to receive the Torah (Shabbat 88b).

Psalm 65 thanks God for rain and harvest: he visits the land, softens it with showers and crowns the year (Psalm 65:9–13). Psalm 67, using the priestly blessing, says "The land has given its crops" (Psalm 67:6), the same promise as Leviticus 26:4, and makes the harvest a reason for the nations to fear God. Jewish communities recite Psalm 67 while counting the Omer between the barley and wheat harvests.

sections.h: Psalm 67: the blessing for the nations
sections.b: Psalm 67 opens with the words of the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) in the third person: "May God show us favor and bless us. May he make his face shine among us" (Psalm 67:1). Its purpose then widens: so that "on the earth they may know your way" (Psalm 67:2).

sections.h: Instruments and processions in Psalms 57, 68 and 71
sections.b: Psalm 57 wakes "harp and lyre" to wake the dawn (Psalm 57:8). Psalm 68 describes a procession into the sanctuary with singers in front, musicians behind and girls beating tambourines between them (Psalm 68:25). Psalm 71 promises praise "on the harp" and "on the lyre" to the Holy One of Israel (Psalm 71:22). Psalm 62 names the guild leader Jeduthun in its title (Psalm 62:0).

Psalm 63 says "Your loyal love is better than life itself" (Psalm 63:3). In Psalm 62 strength and loyal love belong to God together (Psalm 62:11–12), and Psalm 69 bases its plea on "your great loyal love" (Psalm 69:13, 16).

sections.h: The shadow of God's wings in Book Two
sections.b: The image recurs in Psalms 57, 61 and 63: "in the shadow of your wings" the singer takes refuge (Psalm 57:1), lives as a guest (Psalm 61:4) and sings for joy (Psalm 63:7). Many scholars connect it with the cherubim's wings over the ark in the temple.

sections.h: Psalms 69–71: lament from youth to old age
sections.b: Psalms 69, 70 and 71 form a chain of laments. Psalm 69 is the long cry of a man sinking in deep water (Psalm 69:1–2); Psalm 70 is a short urgent call, "God, hurry to me!" (Psalm 70:5); and Psalm 71 is the lament of a man who has trusted God since the womb and asks not to be thrown away in old age (Psalm 71:6, 9). Each ends in praise.

sections.h: "In God I have trusted, and I do not fear" (Psalm 56)
sections.b: Psalm 56 repeats a refrain of trust against fear: "In God I praise his word. In God I have trusted, and I do not fear. What will flesh do to me?" (Psalm 56:4). Psalm 62 says the same with its six lines beginning "Yes": rest is in God alone (Psalm 62:1–2, 5–6).

The speaker of Psalm 69 is mocked because "zeal for your house has eaten me up" (Psalm 69:9). The disciples remembered the line when Jesus drove the traders out of the temple (John 2:17). Psalm 68 pictures the procession into the holy place and kings bringing gifts to the temple (Psalm 68:24–29).

Several psalms of Book Two end with vows: "The vows I made to you are on me, God" (Psalm 56:12), daily vow-keeping (Psalm 61:8), a vow paid in Zion (Psalm 65:1) and burnt offerings brought to pay the vows made in trouble (Psalm 66:13–14).
